name: canonical_json_structure_v1
description: Canonical JSON structural oracle: key ordering and number form. This vector pins the canonical JSON byte rule so an independent verifier can reproduce it as a BLACK BOX, without reading either encoder. Each case gives an input and the exact canonical output, pinned BOTH as text and as expected_canonical_hex (the hex of the UTF-8 output bytes). The hex is authoritative: for the very characters this vector exists to pin, a reader cannot tell from the text alone whether a byte sequence is an escape or a literal, and the hex removes that ambiguity without requiring the consumer to first interpret this file's own JSON escaping. Every expected value here was MEASURED from both the Swift and the Go implementations and confirmed byte-identical; none of it is assumed. Inputs are given as JSON strings, so a control character appears here as its own JSON escape and is decoded to the raw scalar before being handed to the encoder.
rules: Object keys are sorted by UTF-8 byte value, not by Unicode collation and not by insertion order.
Integers are plain decimal with no exponent, no fraction, and no leading plus.
Object keys are restricted to the ASCII repertoire (ARM-48). Non-ASCII object keys are refused with canonical.key-repertoire-unsupported. This constrains KEYS only; string VALUES keep full Unicode.

UNPINNED_key_identity.status: RESOLVED by ARM-48. Previously deferred as DISC-052.
UNPINNED_key_identity.the_case: An object carrying two keys that are DISTINCT byte sequences but Unicode-canonically-equivalent, for example U+00E9 (utf-8 c3a9) and e followed by U+0301 (utf-8 65cc81).
UNPINNED_key_identity.resolution: Both implementations now REFUSE such a pair, because object keys are restricted to the ASCII repertoire and neither key is ASCII. The refusal carries the typed code canonical.key-repertoire-unsupported.
UNPINNED_key_identity.why_the_repertoire_rather_than_detection: Deciding canonical equivalence needs normalization tables. Swift has them implicitly (String equality IS canonical equivalence, which is what caused the original collapse); Go has none in its standard library and the gateway module is deliberately dependency-free. Restricting the repertoire makes equivalence IMPOSSIBLE by construction rather than detected, so both languages refuse exactly the same inputs with no tables and no dependency. Impossibility does not drift between Unicode versions; detection can.
UNPINNED_key_identity.also_resolved: Byte-identical duplicate keys are refused too, with canonical.duplicate-key, on both the encode and strict-decode paths at every depth. Before ARM-48, Go emitted both bindings and Swift collapsed them.
UNPINNED_key_identity.scope: Object KEYS only. String VALUES keep full Unicode and the canonical_json_unicode_v1 oracle is unchanged.

cases.note: Keys are ordered by UTF-8 BYTE value, so uppercase sorts before lowercase.

Byte ordering, not collation: 'Z' (0x5a) sorts before 'a' (0x61). Many locale collations order these the other way, so this pins byte order specifically. This case previously used a non-ASCII key; ARM-48 restricted object keys to ASCII, so that formulation is now invalid and the property is pinned within ASCII.
The empty key is permitted and sorts first.
Plain decimal, no sign, no exponent, no fraction.
9007199254740993 exceeds exact double precision and must survive as an integer, so an implementation routing integers through a float would fail here.
